title: The Free Charting Walkthrough: Learn Tooth Numbering Without a Textbook
meta_desc: A free, step-by-step walkthrough that teaches you to chart a dental visit — tooth numbers, surfaces, and SOAP notes — using our ChairSide practice software. No textbook, no cost, no account.
og_desc: Learn tooth numbering, surfaces, and clinical notes with a free step-by-step walkthrough and practice software full of fake patients you cannot break.
tw_title: Learn dental charting free — no textbook required
tw_desc: Tooth numbers, surfaces, and SOAP notes, explained plainly. Practice on fake patients until it feels easy.
h1: The Free Charting Walkthrough: Learn Tooth Numbering Without a Textbook
lead: Tooth #14, MO surface, prophy adult. If that sentence looks like a license plate, you are exactly who we built this for — and you can start reading it correctly in about ten minutes.
lead_heading: Stuck on a charting question? Ask Amanda.

sections.html:
Charting is writing down what is going on in a patient's mouth and what was done about it, in the patient's official record. Which tooth. Which surface. What procedure. What the dentist observed. It is the part of dental assisting that looks most like a foreign language from the outside and turns out to be the most learnable part once someone slows down and shows you the pattern.

Most people meet charting through a textbook chapter full of diagrams and terminology, get overwhelmed, and decide they are bad at it. That is a teaching problem, not an ability problem. Charting is a small set of rules applied over and over. You do not need to memorize a book. You need reps.

sections.h2: What the free walkthrough actually is
sections.html:
Here is the honest description, because we would rather you know what you are clicking on. The charting walkthrough is a written, step-by-step tutorial. It is not a game and it does not score you. What it does is walk you through charting a visit inside ChairSide, our practice software, with the trainer open in a second tab so you read here and click there.

No account, no cost, no catch. Both the walkthrough and ChairSide are open to anyone. You do not have to be enrolled, you do not have to give us an email address, and there is no timer counting down to a sales page.

Every patient inside ChairSide is fictional. Nothing you type touches a real person's record, and there is no way to break anything. That is the entire point — you get to be clumsy somewhere it costs nothing.

sections.h2: The seven tabs, in plain English
sections.html: Everything in ChairSide lives under one of seven tabs across the top. Once you know what each one is for, the software stops feeling like a maze. Tap any of these to see what it holds.

sections.h2: Tooth numbers: the part everyone thinks is hard
sections.html:
Permanent teeth are numbered 1 through 32, and the counting follows one continuous path. You start at the upper-right back tooth, which is #1. You count across the top to the upper-left, which lands you at #16. Then you drop straight down to the lower-left, which is #17, and come back across to the lower-right, ending at #32.

It is a horseshoe. That is the whole system. The two big teeth at the front and center on top are #8 and #9, which is a handy anchor when you lose your place mid-count.

A note on children's teeth. Baby teeth use letters rather than numbers, and they follow the same clockwise path. If that is where you are headed next, our primary vs. permanent teeth guide lays it out side by side.

sections.h2: Surfaces: five letters that do a lot of work
sections.html:
A tooth is a three-dimensional object, so saying "a filling on #14" is not specific enough. Surfaces tell you which face of the tooth was involved. There are five you will use constantly: M for mesial, toward the front midline. D for distal, toward the back. O for occlusal, the chewing surface. B for buccal or facial, the cheek side. L for lingual, the tongue side.

Now go back and read "MO on #14." A filling on the mesial and occlusal surfaces of tooth 14. Not a license plate anymore. If you want to drill this until it is automatic, the flashcards tool is built for exactly that, and our guide on studying dental anatomy and tooth numbering covers how to space out the practice so it sticks.

sections.h2: SOAP notes and the safety habit that matters most
sections.html:
Clinical notes follow a four-part shape called SOAP. S is subjective, what the patient tells you. O is objective, what you observe or measure. A is assessment, the diagnosis. P is plan, what happens about it. In the walkthrough you pick a note template that matches the visit, the SOAP layout fills in, and you edit the details rather than starting from a blank page.

One habit the walkthrough hammers on, and we will hammer on it here too: on the Clinical tab, click Medical first on every new patient. Allergies, medications, and health alerts live there. Missing an allergy or a heart condition is among the most dangerous mistakes possible in a dental office. Checking Medical before anything else should become so automatic you stop noticing you do it.

Saved notes lock. Once a clinical note is saved it cannot be quietly edited — corrections get added as separate amendments. That is a legal requirement, not a software quirk, and the trainer behaves the same way so the habit transfers.

Once the shape of a note makes sense, the shorthand starts making sense too. Our roundup of common dental charting abbreviations is the natural next stop.

sections.h2: How to actually use it this week
sections.html:
Reading about charting does very little. Doing it badly a dozen times does a great deal. Open the walkthrough on your laptop and ChairSide in a second tab, then work a fictional patient end to end: open the chart, check Medical, read the restorative history, write and save a note, look at the ledger, generate the walkout receipt. That whole loop takes a few minutes.

Then do it again with a different patient and a different note template. The goal is not a perfect note. The goal is for the sequence to stop requiring thought. Assistants who are fluent chairside got there by repetition, and repetition is free here.

sections.h2: Where this fits if you are considering the program
sections.html:
These tools are genuinely free and genuinely useful on their own. Use them whether or not you ever enroll with us — that is not a bargaining position, it is just what they are for.

That said, the difference between practicing charting on fictional patients and doing it in a real operatory is the room. In our twelve-week in-person program in Longview, classes are capped at eight so you get real time with real equipment and real instruments rather than watching from the back. Charting is one thread inside that; you can see the whole picture on the classes page, or come look at the place in person on a free tour. If home-based and self-paced fits your life better, the online program covers the same curriculum.

Beginners who want the gentler on-ramp before touching the software should start with how to chart teeth for beginners.

cards.b: Name, contact information, and insurance. This is where a chart opens when you click a patient from the list on the left.
Today's appointments. In a real office this is the tab the whole day is organized around.

The chart itself, split into four sub-tabs: Restorative (every procedure already done, by tooth and surface), Perio (the gum exam summary), Notes (written clinical notes), and Medical (allergies, medications, health alerts). Click Medical first on every new patient.
Where you write and save a clinical note. Pick a template that matches the visit — Prophy Adult, Restorative, Crown Seat, RCT, SRP and others — and the SOAP layout fills in for you to edit.
X-rays and photos on file for that patient.
Charges, payments, and the running balance for the visit.
The end-of-visit receipt you hand or email the patient on their way out. You can print it or save it as a PDF.

meta_desc: A practical, honest guide to your first day at dental assistant school in Longview — what actually helps, what to leave in the car, and where the official supply list comes from.

tw_title: First day of dental assistant school: what to bring
tw_desc: A short, honest packing guide for day one — plus where the real supply list comes from.
h1: What to Bring to Your First Day of Class (and What to Leave at Home)
lead: Nobody has ever failed a dental assisting program because they brought the wrong notebook. But showing up prepared settles the nerves, and settled nerves are worth a lot on day one.
lead_heading: Not sure what you need for day one? Just ask.

sections.html:
This is not the official supply list. We are not going to publish a dress code or a required-equipment list on a blog post and have you buy the wrong thing off the internet.

The real list comes from the school. After you enroll, you get a welcome email and a supply list with the specifics for your cohort. If you want to confirm anything before then — or you are enrolled and cannot find the email — call or text (903) 913-6444 and ask. That is always the fastest, most accurate answer.

What follows is the general stuff that helps almost anyone on the first day of almost any hands-on program. Treat it as a starting point, not gospel.

sections.h2: The short list that actually matters
sections.html: If you brought nothing but these, you would be fine. Tap each one as you pack it.

sections.h2: Why paper still beats a laptop on day one
sections.html:
You will hear a lot of new vocabulary in the first week — tooth numbers, surfaces, instrument names, procedure abbreviations. Handwriting is slower than typing, and that is precisely the advantage: the bottleneck forces you to summarize instead of transcribing, and summarizing is what makes things stick.

There is also a practical reason. In a hands-on room you are moving between a seat and equipment, gloves come on and off, and a laptop becomes one more thing to manage. A cheap spiral notebook survives all of that.

If you would rather warm up the vocabulary before you walk in, our beginner charting guide and the free flashcards tool cover a lot of the language you will meet in week one. Neither is required. Both make day one quieter.

A shopping cart full of equipment you bought before anyone told you to. This is the most common and most expensive first-day mistake, and it is entirely avoidable. Wait for the supply list. Instruments and materials vary, and guessing means buying twice.

Long or elaborate nails, loose jewelry, and anything dangling. Clinical environments have infection-control and safety reasons for this, and you will get the specifics from the school rather than from us guessing on a blog.

Also leave the assumption that everyone else knows more than you. In a class of eight, someone is a career changer, someone is straight out of high school, someone has been out of a classroom for fifteen years. The room evens out fast.

On nerves: being nervous on day one is not a warning sign. It is what caring about something feels like before you have any evidence you can do it. The evidence comes in week two.

sections.h2: Getting there and the logistics nobody mentions
sections.html:
The campus is at 2800 Gilmer Rd, Suite 106, in Longview. Classes are daytime — call or text (903) 913-6444 for exact hours, since those are confirmed with you directly rather than posted here.

Drive it once before day one if you can, at roughly the time you will actually be driving it. Ten minutes of scouting removes a whole category of first-morning stress. Plan to arrive early enough that parking and finding Suite 106 are not part of your first impression of yourself.

Sort out childcare and your work schedule before the first week rather than during it. The people who struggle in week one are almost never struggling with the material — they are struggling with logistics they meant to figure out later.

sections.h2: What the first day is actually like
sections.html:
Introductions, an overview of how the twelve weeks are structured, the paperwork side of getting started, and a look at the room and the equipment you will be using. It is an orientation day, not a test. Nobody is going to hand you a drill and a stranger.

Classes are capped at eight for a reason. You are not going to be able to hide in the back, and you are also not going to be ignored. For a fuller picture of the early weeks, what to expect on your first day as a dental assistant walks through the rhythm in more detail.

sections.h2: If you have not enrolled yet
sections.html:
Then this post is a little ahead of you, and that is fine — knowing what day one looks like is a reasonable thing to want before committing to anything.

The next in-person cohorts start September 14, September 29, November 9, and November 17. Applying is free and takes a few minutes. What happens after you apply lays out every step between the application and your first morning so there are no surprises, and the calendar has the full schedule.

If you would rather see the room before you decide anything at all, come take a free tour. No pressure, and you can ask about the supply list while you are standing in the place you would be using it.
